extracted.intended_audience: DHS/USCIS adjudicating officers, immigration attorneys, stakeholders, and noncitizen applicants
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and guidance for how DHS will evaluate whether a noncitizen is "likely at any time to become a public charge," with specific rules about long-term institutionalization, Medicaid/HCBS, evidentiary burdens, and how officers should perform predictive determinations under the totality of the circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of long-term institutionalization at government expense
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS will consider the past, current, or likelihood of future long-term institutionalization at government expense in public charge inadmissibility determinations; such institutionalization "is at the core of the public charge statute."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Long-term institutionalization at government expense can be predictive of future dependence on those same benefits. DHS declines to omit long-term institutionalization from consideration. However, such consideration is not alone dispositive and will be evaluated as part of the totality of the circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Long-term institutionalization not dispositive; totality of the circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: Consideration of past or current long-term institutionalization is not alone dispositive of a public charge determination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS will perform a totality of the circumstances analysis, taking into account recency and duration of institutionalization along with other factors. Officers should not treat past/current institutionalization as automatically rendering a noncitizen inadmissible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusion of HCBS from public charge consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS will not consider Home and Community-Based Services (HCBS) in public charge inadmissibility determinations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS retains the clarification that HCBS are not to be included. DHS will make this point clear in sub-regulatory guidance and public communications to mitigate chilling effects. Evidence that institutionalization occurred due to lack of HCBS availability may, however, be relevant when showing institutionalization violated rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: General exclusion of Medicaid/Medicare (except long-term institutionalization)
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS will generally not consider non-cash public benefits, including government-funded healthcare coverage such as Medicaid or Medicare, except for Medicaid-funded long-term institutionalization at government expense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The regulatory text clearly identifies the only healthcare service included in the public charge determination: long-term institutionalization at government expense. Receipt of Medicaid for preventive services or COVID-19 treatment will not be considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of evidence that institutionalization violated disability rights
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS will consider credible and probative evidence that an individual was institutionalized in violation of disability laws; such evidence will tend to offset evidence of current or past institutionalization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence may include HCBS waiting lists, state compliance with disability rights laws, and other indicators that institutionalization resulted from lack of alternatives. DHS will not shift burdens; applicants bear the burden to submit such evidence to demonstrate eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recency and duration of institutionalization matter
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS will look at the recency and duration of long-term institutionalization when evaluating its relevance to a public charge determination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS distinguished long-term institutionalization from periodic or intermittent stays. The more recent and prolonged the institutionalization, the more weight it may carry in the totality analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predictive determinations must be evidence-based; avoid undue speculation
rubrics_metrics.description: Officers should make predictive public charge determinations on the basis of available evidence and without unduly speculating as to an applicant's future circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS acknowledges difficulty predicting distant future events; e.g., a healthy young applicant is unlikely to be found inadmissible because they might need nursing home care decades later. But older applicants with serious health conditions and limited resources may be reasonably predicted to be likely to need government-funded institutional care.

rubrics_metrics.name: Household assets, resources, and financial status factor
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS will consider household assets and resources, including income and in-kind contributions, as part of the assets/resources factor in the totality of the circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS may consider that a household member subject to public charge is a primary caregiver providing in-kind support even if not contributing income. Insufficient assets that result from a household member leaving the U.S. (e.g., due to inadmissibility) may also be considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: "Impact on the family" not a relevant factor
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS will not consider the impact of an inadmissibility determination on the family as a relevant factor in the public charge analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although DHS may consider household assets/resources, the broader "impact on the family" does not make a noncitizen more or less likely to become primarily dependent on government for subsistence and therefore is excluded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant bears burden of proof to establish eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The applicant for admission or adjustment of status has the burden of proof to establish eligibility for the requested immigration benefit; DHS will not shift the burden to itself to demonstrate that institutionalization was not in violation of an individual's rights or that alternatives were available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a noncitizen wishes DHS to treat institutionalization as having resulted from lack of alternatives, they should submit credible evidence (e.g., HCBS waiting lists, state noncompliance) to support that claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusions from definition of long-term institutionalization (short-term rehab, imprisonment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain settings and stays—such as short-term rehabilitation and imprisonment—do not qualify as long-term institutionalization at government expense under 8 CFR 212.21.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS provided regulatory text explaining the types of institutionalizations that do not qualify. Commitment to a facility resulting from a criminal proceeding would not be considered long-term institutionalization at government expense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of civil commitment and criminal-related commitment
rubrics_metrics.description: Involuntary civil commitment in criminal proceedings (e.g., observation or commitment pending or after a finding of incompetence) is not being added as an exception; however, commitment resulting from criminal proceedings is not considered long-term institutionalization at government expense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS may consider the underlying medical/psychiatric condition in the totality of the circumstances (health factor) if identified on Form I-693, but will not equate criminal incarceration with institutional long-term care for public charge purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Receipt of SSI is considered public cash assistance
rubrics_metrics.description: If a noncitizen is receiving SSI, then they are receiving public cash assistance for income maintenance, which DHS would consider in a public charge inadmissibility determination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Receipt of HCBS alone would not be considered, but concurrent receipt of cash benefits like SSI is treated differently and may be relevant to the assets/resources analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of family's role in providing care/support
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS may consider whether a noncitizen is being cared for and/or supported by family or sponsor(s) when there is evidence a medical condition impacts their ability to care for themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Family care/support can be relevant evidence under the totality of circumstances, including consideration of household-level assets and in-kind caregiving contributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural avenues (RFE/NOID, motions, appeals) remain applicable
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS will not create a special appellate process for public charge determinations; USCIS retains discretion to issue Requests for Evidence (RFE) or Notices of Intent to Deny (NOID), and applicants may file motions to reopen/reconsider or pursue appeals/motions as provided in existing regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If evidence is missing or insufficient, officers can issue RFEs/NOIDs per 8 CFR 103.2(b)(8); no administrative appeal from denial of adjustment of status, but motions and AAO certification or immigration court review may be available where applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mitigating chilling effects via guidance and communications
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS intends to mitigate chilling effects by clarifying in guidance and communication materials that Medicaid (other than long-term institutionalization) is not considered in public charge determinations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS will make clear public communications and sub-regulatory guidance to ensure the public understands the limited scope of what health benefits are considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of availability of alternatives to institutionalization when assessing violations
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS may consider evidence regarding availability of alternatives to institutionalization (such as HCBS waiting lists, average time to placement, transition services, and States' compliance with disability rights laws) when evaluating whether institutionalization was in violation of an individual's rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such evidence can offset weight given to past/current institutionalization but must be submitted by the applicant, as DHS will not undertake to demonstrate lack of alternatives on its own.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal proximity and applicant characteristics in likelihood assessments
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS will weigh applicant characteristics (age, serious health conditions, limited resources) and temporal proximity when assessing the likelihood that an individual will at any time become primarily dependent on government subsistence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A young, healthy applicant likely will not be found inadmissible based on the distant possibility of future nursing-home care, but an older person with serious conditions and limited resources may be found likely to become a public charge in part due to probable need for nursing home care.
